units.en: Containers and images (OCI, image layers, registries, runtimes)
Containers, Images, OCI and Runtimes

Containers package an application plus its dependencies into a portable, isolated unit; images are the immutable templates they run from.

  • Containers share the host kernel and isolate using Linux namespaces (isolation) and cgroups (resource limits). They are lighter-weight than VMs (no guest OS).
  • An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance with a thin writable layer on top.
  • Image layers: images are built in stacked, read-only layers (one per build instruction). Layers are cached and shared across images, saving space and speeding builds/pulls.
  • OCI (Open Container Initiative): a CNCF-related standards body defining the image-spec (image format), runtime-spec (how to run containers), and distribution-spec (registry API). Ensures portability across tools.
  • Registries store and distribute images (e.g., Docker Hub, GHCR, Quay, ECR). Images are referenced as registry/repo:tag; digests (sha256) pin exact content.
  • Container runtimes: high-level runtimes like containerd and CRI-O manage image pull, storage, and lifecycle and implement the CRI (Container Runtime Interface). Low-level runtime runc actually creates the container per the OCI runtime-spec.
  • Exam tip: Docker is no longer the cluster runtime; dockershim was removed in Kubernetes 1.24. Kubelet talks to runtimes via the CRI.
  • Exam tip: OCI = image + runtime + distribution specs; CRI = how kubelet calls the runtime.
Pods and the pod lifecycle
Pods and the Pod Lifecycle

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes and the basic unit of scheduling.

  • A Pod wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace (same IP and port space, reachable via localhost) and can share storage volumes.
  • Pods are ephemeral: they are not healed in place. If a node dies, controllers create new Pods rather than reviving old ones.
  • Each Pod gets its own unique IP. Containers in a Pod are always scheduled together on the same node.
  • Init containers run to completion, in order, before app containers start (setup tasks). Sidecar containers run alongside the main container (logging, proxy).

Pod phases (status.phase):

  • Pending: accepted but not all containers running (e.g., pulling image, awaiting scheduling).
  • Running: bound to a node, at least one container running.
  • Succeeded: all containers exited 0 and won't restart.
  • Failed: all containers terminated, at least one failed.
  • Unknown: state can't be determined (often node comms lost).
  • Probes: liveness (restart if unhealthy), readiness (remove from Service endpoints until ready), startup (protects slow-starting apps).
  • restartPolicy: Always (default), OnFailure, Never.
  • Exam tip: You rarely create bare Pods directly; use controllers (Deployment, Job, etc.) for self-healing.
Deployments, ReplicaSets and rolling updates
Deployments, ReplicaSets and Rolling Updates

Deployments provide declarative, self-healing management of stateless Pods and handle versioned updates.

  • A ReplicaSet ensures a specified number of replica Pods are running, using a label selector. It replaces failed/deleted Pods to maintain the desired count.
  • A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and adds rolling updates and rollbacks. You usually manage Deployments, not ReplicaSets directly.
  • On an update (e.g., new image), the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually scales it up while scaling the old one down.

Update strategies:

  • RollingUpdate (default): incremental replacement with zero downtime. Controlled by maxSurge (extra Pods allowed) and maxUnavailable (Pods that can be down).
  • Recreate: terminates all old Pods, then creates new ones (causes downtime).
  • Rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> reverts to a previous ReplicaSet. Check progress with kubectl rollout status.
  • Scale with kubectl scale or by editing replicas.
  • Exam tip: Deployment → manages ReplicaSet → manages Pods. ReplicaSet handles count; Deployment handles version rollout/rollback.
  • Exam tip: Deployments are for stateless apps; use StatefulSets for stateful ones.
Services and basic networking (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, cluster DNS)
Services, Service Types and Cluster DNS

A Service provides a stable network endpoint and load-balances traffic across a changing set of Pods selected by labels.

  • Pods are ephemeral with changing IPs; a Service gives a stable virtual IP (ClusterIP) and DNS name in front of them.
  • Services use a label selector to find backing Pods, tracked as Endpoints / EndpointSlices.

Service types:

  • ClusterIP (default): internal-only virtual IP, reachable inside the cluster.
  • NodePort: exposes the Service on a static port (range 30000-32767) on every node's IP; builds on ClusterIP.
  • LoadBalancer: provisions an external cloud load balancer; builds on NodePort. Typical for cloud external access.
  • ExternalName: maps the Service to an external DNS name via a CNAME (no proxying).
  • Cluster DNS (CoreDNS): gives Services DNS names like service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Pods resolve Services by name automatically.
  • Ingress manages external HTTP/HTTPS routing (host/path rules) to Services; needs an Ingress controller. Newer Gateway API is its successor.
  • Exam tip: LoadBalancer ⊃ NodePort ⊃ ClusterIP (each builds on the previous).
  • Exam tip: CoreDNS is the default cluster DNS; the CNI plugin implements pod networking, not Services.
ConfigMaps and Secrets
ConfigMaps and Secrets

ConfigMaps and Secrets decouple configuration and sensitive data from container images, following the config-from-environment principle.

  • ConfigMap: stores non-confidential key/value configuration data (settings, config files, URLs).
  • Secret: stores sensitive data (passwords, tokens, keys, TLS certs). Same idea as ConfigMaps but for secrets.

How they're consumed by Pods:

  • As environment variables (individual keys or all keys via envFrom).
  • As mounted volume files (each key becomes a file).

Key facts about Secrets:

  • Secret data is base64-encoded, NOT encrypted by default. Base64 is encoding, not security.
  • Secrets are stored in etcd; enable encryption at rest for real protection.
  • Use RBAC to limit who can read Secrets.
  • Secret types include Opaque (default), kubernetes.io/tls, and kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson (image pull).
  • Exam tip: The exam loves asking that Secrets are only base64-encoded by default — not encrypted unless encryption at rest is configured.
  • Exam tip: Both can be injected as env vars or files; both are namespaced objects.
Namespaces, labels, selectors and annotations
Namespaces, Labels, Selectors and Annotations

These mechanisms organize, group, and identify objects within a cluster.

  • Namespaces: provide logical isolation and grouping of resources within one cluster (e.g., teams, environments). They scope names and enable resource quotas and RBAC boundaries.
  • Default namespaces: default, kube-system (control-plane components), kube-public, kube-node-lease.
  • Not everything is namespaced: Nodes, PersistentVolumes, and Namespaces themselves are cluster-scoped.
  • Labels: key/value pairs attached to objects for identification and grouping. They are meaningful to users and used by selectors (e.g., app=web, env=prod).
  • Selectors: query objects by their labels. Equality-based (=, !=) and set-based (in, notin, exists). Services, Deployments, and ReplicaSets use selectors to find their Pods.
  • Annotations: key/value pairs for non-identifying metadata (build info, tooling config, descriptions). Not used by selectors; can hold larger/structured data.
  • Exam tip: Labels are for selecting/grouping; annotations are for arbitrary metadata that tools read, never for selection.
  • Exam tip: Namespaces give isolation but are not a strong security boundary by themselves; pair with RBAC, quotas, and network policies.
Control plane components (kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, controller-manager, cloud-controller-manager)
Control Plane Components

The control plane makes global decisions about the cluster and maintains the desired state.

  • kube-apiserver: the front end of the control plane and the only component that talks to etcd. Exposes the Kubernetes REST API; all components and kubectl communicate through it. Handles authn, authz, and admission control. It is stateless and horizontally scalable.
  • etcd: distributed, consistent key-value store that is the cluster's single source of truth (all cluster state/config). Should be backed up; loss of etcd = loss of cluster state.
  • kube-scheduler: watches for unscheduled Pods and assigns each to a node based on resource requests, affinity/anti-affinity, taints/tolerations, and constraints. It decides placement; it does not start the Pod.
  • kube-controller-manager: runs the controllers that drive actual state toward desired state via reconciliation loops (Node, ReplicaSet, Deployment, Job, EndpointSlice controllers, etc.).
  • cloud-controller-manager: integrates with the cloud provider — manages cloud load balancers, nodes, and routes. Decouples cloud-specific logic from core Kubernetes.
  • Exam tip: Only the API server reads/writes etcd; everything goes through the API server.
  • Exam tip: Scheduler chooses the node; the kubelet on that node actually runs the Pod.
  • Exam tip: Kubernetes is built on the reconciliation loop: observe → diff desired vs actual → act.
Node components (kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime)
Node Components

Node (worker) components run on every node and keep Pods running and networked.

  • kubelet: the node agent. Registers the node, receives Pod specs from the API server, and ensures the described containers are running and healthy. It runs probes and reports node/Pod status back. It manages Pods, not containers it didn't create.
  • kube-proxy: maintains network rules on each node to implement Services, enabling traffic forwarding and load balancing to backend Pods. Uses iptables or IPVS (or eBPF via some CNIs). It is a per-node network proxy, optional if the CNI handles Service routing.
  • Container runtime: actually runs the containers (e.g., containerd, CRI-O). Kubelet talks to it via the CRI.
  • Networking on nodes is provided by a CNI plugin (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Flannel), which assigns Pod IPs and enables pod-to-pod connectivity.
  • Exam tip: kubelet ↔ Pods/health; kube-proxy ↔ Service networking; runtime ↔ runs containers.
  • Exam tip: The kubelet does not manage the network or implement Services — that's kube-proxy/CNI.
  • Exam tip: Every node runs kubelet, kube-proxy, and a container runtime; control-plane nodes also run control-plane components.
The Kubernetes API and declarative object management with kubectl
The Kubernetes API and Declarative Management with kubectl

Kubernetes is declarative and API-centric: you describe desired state, and controllers continuously reconcile toward it.

  • kube-apiserver exposes a RESTful API; every object has a spec (desired state) and status (current state, set by the system).
  • Objects are grouped into API groups and versions (e.g., apps/v1, v1 core). Manifests declare apiVersion, kind, metadata, and spec.
  • Declarative management: kubectl apply -f file.yaml declares desired state; Kubernetes computes and makes the changes. Preferred for GitOps/version control.
  • Imperative management: commands like kubectl create, run, delete, scale act directly — good for quick tasks but harder to track.

Common kubectl commands:

  • kubectl get / describe — inspect objects.
  • kubectl apply -f — declarative create/update.
  • kubectl logs, kubectl exec — debug containers.
  • kubectl explain — discover field schemas.
  • CRDs (CustomResourceDefinitions) extend the API with new object kinds, often paired with operators (custom controllers).
  • Exam tip: Prefer apply (declarative) over imperative commands for reproducibility.
  • Exam tip: You set spec; the system manages status. Controllers reconcile spec → status.
Scheduling (nodeSelector, affinity/anti-affinity, taints and tolerations, resource requests and limits)
Scheduling: Placement Controls and Resources

The kube-scheduler places Pods on nodes; several mechanisms influence or constrain where Pods land.

  • Resource requests: the minimum CPU/memory a Pod needs; used by the scheduler to find a node with enough capacity (drives placement). Unschedulable if no node fits.
  • Resource limits: the maximum a container may use. Exceeding a memory limit causes OOMKill; CPU over-limit is throttled.
  • nodeSelector: simplest constraint — schedule only on nodes with matching labels.
  • Affinity / anti-affinity: more expressive rules. Node affinity attracts Pods to labeled nodes; Pod affinity co-locates Pods; Pod anti-affinity spreads them apart. Modes: requiredDuringScheduling (hard) vs preferredDuringScheduling (soft).
  • Taints and tolerations: a taint on a node repels Pods; a Pod needs a matching toleration to be scheduled there. Effects: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute (evicts existing Pods).
  • Exam tip: Taints/tolerations are about nodes repelling Pods (opt-out); affinity is about Pods being attracted (opt-in). A toleration only allows, it doesn't force placement.
  • Exam tip: Requests affect scheduling; limits affect runtime enforcement. QoS classes (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort) derive from requests/limits.
Storage basics (Volumes, PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims)
Storage: Volumes, PVs and PVCs

Kubernetes storage decouples data lifetime from the ephemeral container, with abstractions for persistence and provisioning.

  • Volumes: attached to a Pod; they outlive container restarts but are tied to the Pod's lifecycle (e.g., emptyDir is deleted when the Pod is removed). Shared among containers in the Pod.
  • PersistentVolume (PV): a cluster-scoped piece of storage provisioned by an admin or dynamically. Its lifecycle is independent of any Pod.
  • PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC): a namespaced user request for storage (size + access mode). Kubernetes binds the PVC to a matching PV; the Pod mounts the PVC.
  • StorageClass: enables dynamic provisioning — a PVC referencing a StorageClass auto-creates a PV via a provisioner (often a CSI driver).

Access modes: ReadWriteOnce (one node), ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany, ReadWriteOncePod.

  • Reclaim policy: Retain (keep data), Delete (remove backing storage). Default for dynamic PVs is often Delete.
  • CSI (Container Storage Interface): standard for plugging external storage systems into Kubernetes.
  • Exam tip: PVCs request storage; PVs provide it; StorageClass dynamically provisions PVs. PV = cluster-scoped, PVC = namespaced.
Other workloads (StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs)
Workload Controllers: StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs

Beyond Deployments, Kubernetes offers specialized controllers for different workload patterns.

  • StatefulSet: manages stateful applications needing stable identity. Provides stable, ordered Pod names (web-0, web-1), stable network IDs, and persistent per-Pod storage (via volumeClaimTemplates). Pods are created/scaled/deleted in order. Used for databases, clustered apps (e.g., Kafka, Cassandra).
  • DaemonSet: ensures a copy of a Pod runs on every node (or a subset). Ideal for node-level agents: log collectors, monitoring agents, CNI/network plugins, storage daemons. New nodes automatically get the Pod.
  • Job: runs Pods to completion for batch/one-off tasks. Retries on failure and tracks successful completions (completions, parallelism). Pods are not restarted indefinitely.
  • CronJob: creates Jobs on a time schedule using cron syntax (e.g., backups, reports). It's a scheduled wrapper around Jobs.
  • Exam tip: Deployment = stateless; StatefulSet = stateful with stable identity/storage; DaemonSet = one per node; Job = run to completion; CronJob = scheduled Job.
  • Exam tip: Only StatefulSet gives ordered, stable network and storage identity; DaemonSet's defining trait is one Pod per node.
Containers and images
What is the OCI (Open Container Initiative)?

An open governance project under the Linux Foundation that defines industry standards for containers, primarily the Image Specification (image format) and Runtime Specification (how to run a container). It ensures interoperability across tools and runtimes.
Containers and images
What are container image layers and how are they stored?

An image is built from stacked, read-only filesystem layers, each representing a change (e.g., a Dockerfile instruction). Layers are content-addressable and shared/cached across images, so common layers are downloaded and stored only once.
Containers and images
What is a container registry?
A service that stores and distributes container images (e.g., Docker Hub, Quay, GHCR, ECR). Clients push images to and pull them from a registry; images are referenced by name and tag or by digest.
Containers and images
What is a container runtime and what role does CRI play?
A runtime starts and manages containers from images. Kubernetes talks to runtimes (e.g., containerd, CRI-O) through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), a standard gRPC API the kubelet uses.
Containers and images
Difference between a container image and a running container?
An image is a static, read-only template (layers + metadata). A container is a running (or runnable) instance of that image, adding a thin writable layer on top for runtime changes.
Pods and the pod lifecycle
What is a Pod in Kubernetes?
The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. A Pod is one or more containers that share the same network namespace (IP and ports) and storage volumes, and are scheduled together on a single node.
Pods and the pod lifecycle
List the Pod lifecycle phases.
Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, and Unknown. Pending means accepted but not all containers are running yet; Succeeded/Failed are terminal states for all containers.
Pods and the pod lifecycle
What is an init container?
A container that runs to completion before the app (regular) containers start. Init containers run sequentially and are used for setup tasks like waiting on dependencies or preparing data.
Pods and the pod lifecycle
What are the three container probe types?
Liveness (restart container if it fails), Readiness (remove Pod from Service endpoints until it passes), and Startup (gives slow-starting apps time before liveness/readiness apply).
Pods and the pod lifecycle
What does a Pod's restartPolicy control, and what are the options?
It controls whether containers are restarted by the kubelet. Options are Always (default), OnFailure, and Never. It applies to all containers in the Pod.
Deployments, ReplicaSets and rolling updates
What does a Deployment do?
A Deployment provides declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. It manages stateless workloads, handling rollouts, rollbacks, and scaling by creating and managing ReplicaSets.
Deployments, ReplicaSets and rolling updates
What is a ReplicaSet's job?

A ReplicaSet ensures a specified number of identical Pod replicas are running at all times, creating or deleting Pods to match the desired replica count. It is usually managed by a Deployment, not directly.
Deployments, ReplicaSets and rolling updates
How does a RollingUpdate deployment strategy work?
It gradually replaces old Pods with new ones, controlled by maxSurge (extra Pods allowed above desired) and maxUnavailable (Pods allowed to be down). This enables zero-downtime updates.
Deployments, ReplicaSets and rolling updates
How do you roll back a Deployment?
Use 'kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>'. Deployments keep a revision history of previous ReplicaSets, allowing rollback to a prior revision.
Deployments, ReplicaSets and rolling updates
What is the difference between RollingUpdate and Recreate strategies?

RollingUpdate (default) incrementally replaces Pods for zero downtime. Recreate terminates all existing Pods before creating new ones, causing downtime but ensuring no two versions run simultaneously.
Services and basic networking
What is a Kubernetes Service?
An abstraction that defines a stable network endpoint (virtual IP and DNS name) for a logical set of Pods selected by labels, load-balancing traffic across them even as Pods come and go.
Services and basic networking
What is a ClusterIP Service?
The default Service type. It exposes the Service on an internal cluster-only virtual IP, reachable only from within the cluster. Used for internal communication between workloads.
Services and basic networking
What is a NodePort Service?
Exposes the Service on a static port (default range 30000-32767) on every node's IP. External traffic to <NodeIP>:<NodePort> is routed to the Service. It builds on ClusterIP.
Services and basic networking
What is a LoadBalancer Service?
Exposes the Service externally using a cloud provider's external load balancer, which routes to the NodePort/ClusterIP. It is the standard way to expose services publicly in cloud environments.
Services and basic networking
What provides cluster DNS and how are Services resolved?
CoreDNS (the default DNS server) provides in-cluster DNS. Services get a record like <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, letting Pods reach Services by name.
ConfigMaps and Secrets
What is a ConfigMap?

An API object that stores non-confidential configuration data as key-value pairs. It can be consumed by Pods as environment variables, command-line args, or mounted files, decoupling config from images.
ConfigMaps and Secrets
What is a Secret and how is it stored by default?

A Secret stores sensitive data (passwords, tokens, keys). By default its data is only base64-encoded (not encrypted) in etcd; encryption at rest must be enabled separately. It is consumed like a ConfigMap.
ConfigMaps and Secrets
Is base64 encoding the same as encryption for Secrets?
No. Base64 is reversible encoding, not encryption, and provides no real security. Genuine protection requires enabling etcd encryption at rest and proper RBAC.
ConfigMaps and Secrets
Name two ways a Pod can consume a ConfigMap or Secret.
As environment variables injected into containers, or as files mounted via a volume. Secrets can also be used as imagePullSecrets for registry authentication.
Namespaces, labels, selectors and annotations
What is a Namespace?

A virtual cluster that provides a scope for names and a way to divide cluster resources among users/teams. It enables isolation and resource quotas. Some objects (like nodes) are cluster-scoped and not namespaced.
Namespaces, labels, selectors and annotations
What are the default namespaces in a cluster?
default (for user objects with no namespace), kube-system (control plane and system components), kube-public (readable by all, often cluster info), and kube-node-lease (node heartbeat lease objects).
Namespaces, labels, selectors and annotations
What is the difference between labels and annotations?

Labels are key-value pairs used to identify and select objects (queryable via selectors). Annotations attach arbitrary non-identifying metadata (not used for selection), often for tools and libraries.
Namespaces, labels, selectors and annotations
What are selectors used for?
Selectors filter objects by their labels. Services, Deployments, and ReplicaSets use label selectors to determine which Pods they manage or route to (e.g., 'app=nginx').
Control plane components
What is the kube-apiserver?

The front end of the control plane and the only component that talks to etcd. It exposes the Kubernetes REST API, validates and processes requests, and serves as the central hub all other components communicate through.
Control plane components
What is etcd's role?
etcd is the consistent, highly-available distributed key-value store that holds all cluster state and configuration. It is the cluster's single source of truth and should be backed up.
Control plane components
What does the kube-scheduler do?
It watches for newly created Pods with no assigned node and selects an appropriate node for them based on resource requirements, constraints (affinity, taints), and policies.
Control plane components
What is the kube-controller-manager?
A control plane component that runs controller processes (e.g., Node, ReplicaSet, Job, EndpointSlice controllers) which watch cluster state and work to drive it toward the desired state.
Control plane components
What does the cloud-controller-manager do?
It runs controllers that integrate with the underlying cloud provider's API, managing cloud-specific logic like load balancers, nodes, and routes, keeping cloud-dependent code separate from the core.
Node components
What is the kubelet?

The primary node agent that runs on every node. It registers the node, watches the API server for Pods assigned to it, and ensures the containers described in PodSpecs are running and healthy via the CRI.
Node components
What does kube-proxy do?
A network proxy running on each node that maintains network rules (using iptables or IPVS) to implement Service abstraction, routing traffic to the correct backend Pods.
Node components
What is the container runtime's role on a node?
It is the software responsible for pulling images and running containers (e.g., containerd, CRI-O). The kubelet uses it through the CRI to manage container lifecycle.
Node components
Which node component handles Pod-to-Pod load balancing for Services?
kube-proxy. It programs the node's networking rules so traffic to a Service's virtual IP is distributed across the Service's backend Pods.
The Kubernetes API and declarative object management
What is declarative object management with kubectl?

You describe the desired state in manifest files and apply them with 'kubectl apply -f', letting Kubernetes reconcile actual state to match. This contrasts with imperative commands like 'kubectl create' or 'kubectl run'.
The Kubernetes API and declarative object management
What are the four required top-level fields in most Kubernetes manifests?
apiVersion, kind, metadata, and spec. The cluster fills in status to report the observed state of the object.
The Kubernetes API and declarative object management
What does the Kubernetes controller reconciliation loop do?

Controllers continuously compare the desired state (spec) against the actual state (status) and take actions to converge them. This control loop is the foundation of Kubernetes' self-healing behavior.
The Kubernetes API and declarative object management
What is a CustomResourceDefinition (CRD)?
A CRD extends the Kubernetes API by defining new custom resource types, which can then be managed declaratively with kubectl just like built-in objects. CRDs are the basis of the Operator pattern.
Scheduling
What is a nodeSelector?
The simplest scheduling constraint: a Pod field specifying key-value labels a node must have for the Pod to be scheduled there. The Pod will only run on nodes matching all specified labels.
Scheduling
What is the difference between node affinity and pod (anti-)affinity?

Node affinity attracts Pods to nodes based on node labels (more expressive than nodeSelector). Pod affinity/anti-affinity schedules Pods relative to other Pods' labels, co-locating or spreading them apart.
Scheduling
How do taints and tolerations work together?

A taint on a node repels Pods that do not tolerate it. A toleration on a Pod allows (but does not require) it to be scheduled onto a node with a matching taint. Together they keep unwanted Pods off specific nodes.
Scheduling
What is the difference between a resource request and a limit?

A request is the amount of CPU/memory guaranteed and used by the scheduler to place a Pod. A limit is the maximum a container may use; exceeding a memory limit causes an OOM kill, and CPU above the limit is throttled.
Other workloads
What is a StatefulSet and how does it differ from a Deployment?

A StatefulSet manages stateful applications, providing stable, unique network identities, ordered deployment/scaling, and stable persistent storage per Pod. Unlike Deployments, Pods are not interchangeable and have ordinal names (e.g., web-0, web-1).
Containers & Images
What does the acronym OCI stand for in the context of cloud native containers?

OCI stands for the Open Container Initiative, a Linux Foundation project that defines open standards for container image format, runtime, and distribution. The other expansions are not real organizations or standards.

Containers & Images
A container image is best described as which of the following?

An image is a static, read-only package of code and dependencies; a container is the running instance of that image. Containers share the host kernel rather than bundling their own, which distinguishes them from virtual machines.
A read-only template containing the application code, runtime, libraries, and dependencies needed to run a container
A running process with its own isolated network and filesystem namespaces
A lightweight virtual machine that includes its own guest operating system kernel
A configuration file that tells Kubernetes how many replicas of a Pod to run
Containers & Images
Container images are composed of layers. Which statement about image layers is correct?

Image layers are read-only and stacked; when a container starts, a thin writable layer is added on top for runtime changes. Layers are content-addressable and can be cached and shared across images, which is why distinct images sharing a base reuse layers.
Each layer represents a set of filesystem changes and is read-only, while a writable layer is added on top when a container runs
Each layer is fully writable, allowing the running container to permanently modify the base image
Layers must be rebuilt from scratch every time and cannot be shared between images
An image can contain at most one layer to keep it lightweight

What is the primary purpose of a container registry such as Docker Hub or a private Harbor instance?

A registry is a storage and distribution service for images; builders push images to it and nodes pull from it. Scheduling is the kube-scheduler's job, and executing containers is the runtime's job, not the registry's.
To store and distribute container images so they can be pushed by builders and pulled by runtimes
To schedule Pods onto worker nodes based on resource requests
To provide the writable layer that a container uses at runtime
To act as the container runtime that executes images on each node

Kubernetes communicates with the container runtime on each node through which standardized interface?

The kubelet talks to the container runtime via the CRI (Container Runtime Interface). CNI handles networking and CSI handles storage, while the OCI runtime spec is a lower-level standard the runtimes themselves implement rather than the interface Kubernetes uses.
CRI (Container Runtime Interface)
CNI (Container Network Interface)
CSI (Container Storage Interface)

Since Kubernetes removed the dockershim, which of the following is a commonly used CRI-compatible container runtime in clusters today?

containerd (and CRI-O) are CRI-compatible runtimes widely used after dockershim's removal in Kubernetes 1.24. kube-proxy handles Service networking, etcd is the cluster datastore, and kubelet is the node agent that calls the runtime, not a runtime itself.
containerd
kube-proxy
etcd
kubelet
Containers & Images
In an image reference like 'nginx:1.25', what does the part after the colon ('1.25') represent?

The portion after the colon is the tag, a human-readable label (often a version) for an image. The registry host appears before the repository name, and the immutable content digest is a SHA-256 hash referenced with '@sha256:...'.
The image tag, which identifies a specific version or variant of the image
The registry hostname where the image is stored
The unique content digest of the image manifest
The number of layers contained in the image
Containers & Images
A team wants to ensure that a Pod always runs the exact same image bits, even if someone overwrites a tag in the registry. What is the most reliable way to reference the image?

A digest (image@sha256:...) is content-addressable and immutable, so it always resolves to identical bits regardless of tag changes. Tags (including version tags) can be re-pushed to point at different content, and 'latest' is especially mutable; imagePullPolicy: Never only affects caching, not which content a tag maps to.
Pin the image by its immutable content digest (e.g., image@sha256:...)
Use the 'latest' tag so Kubernetes always fetches the newest build
Set imagePullPolicy to Never so the node keeps its cached copy

Why Container Orchestration Exists

Containers are lightweight and portable, but running them at scale by hand is impractical. Orchestration automates deployment, scaling, and operations of containers across many machines.

  • The problem: manually starting containers, restarting crashes, load-balancing, rolling updates, and placement across nodes does not scale past a few hosts.
  • Orchestrator responsibilities: scheduling (placing workloads on suitable nodes), self-healing (restarting/replacing failed containers), horizontal scaling, service discovery and load balancing, rolling updates/rollbacks, and config/secret management.
  • Declarative model: you declare a desired state; the orchestrator runs a continuous reconciliation loop to make actual state match. Kubernetes uses controllers for this.
  • Kubernetes is the CNCF graduated, de facto standard orchestrator (donated by Google, based on Borg). Alternatives: Docker Swarm, HashiCorp Nomad.
  • Key benefit: abstracts away individual servers; you treat the cluster as a single pool of compute.

Exam tips

  • Know declarative vs imperative: declarative (desired state) is the Kubernetes-native approach.
  • Self-healing and reconciliation loops are recurring KCNA themes.
  • The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes is the Pod, not the container.
  • Orchestration enables resilience, scalability, and efficient resource utilization without manual intervention.

  • High-level runtimes (CRI-compatible): containerd (CNCF graduated) and CRI-O. They pull images, manage container lifecycle, and call a low-level runtime.
  • Low-level runtime: runc is the reference OCI runtime that actually creates the container using Linux namespaces and cgroups.
  • OCI (Open Container Initiative): defines open standards for the image-spec (image format) and runtime-spec (how to run a container). Hosted under the Linux Foundation.
  • Dockershim removed: as of Kubernetes v1.24, Docker is no longer a directly supported runtime. Docker-built images still run fine (they are OCI-compliant).

Kubernetes networking is built on a flat model where every Pod gets its own IP and can reach every other Pod without NAT.

  • CNI (Container Network Interface): a CNCF spec/plugin standard the kubelet uses to attach Pods to the network. Kubernetes ships no built-in network; you install a CNI plugin.
  • Common CNI plugins: Calico, Cilium (eBPF-based), Flannel, Weave Net. Some (Calico, Cilium) also enforce NetworkPolicies.
  • kube-proxy: runs on each node and implements Service virtual IPs by programming iptables or IPVS rules, load-balancing traffic to backing Pods. Cilium can replace kube-proxy with eBPF.
  • Cluster DNS (CoreDNS): provides service discovery; Services get DNS names like my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster.local.

    • NodePort — exposes a port on every node.
    • LoadBalancer — provisions an external cloud load balancer.
    • ExternalName — maps to an external DNS name (CNAME), no proxying.

A service mesh adds a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication, moving networking concerns out of application code.

  • Sidecar pattern: a proxy container (often Envoy) is injected alongside each Pod and intercepts all inbound/outbound traffic transparently.
  • Data plane vs control plane: the data plane is the set of sidecar proxies that carry traffic; the control plane configures and manages them.
  • Core capabilities:
    • mTLS — automatic mutual TLS encryption and identity between services (zero-trust).
    • Traffic management — canary releases, A/B routing, traffic splitting, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking.
    • Observability — metrics, distributed tracing, and access logs out of the box.
  • Istio: feature-rich, uses Envoy sidecars (also offers ambient/sidecar-less mode). Linkerd: CNCF graduated, lightweight, simpler, uses its own Rust micro-proxy.

    • ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) — a single Pod.

Cloud native fundamentals and the CNCF landscape
Cloud Native Fundamentals & the CNCF Landscape

Cloud native is an approach to building and running scalable applications in modern, dynamic environments like public, private, and hybrid clouds.

  • CNCF definition pillars: containers, service meshes, microservices, immutable infrastructure, and declarative APIs.
  • Goal: systems that are resilient, manageable, and observable, allowing frequent, low-effort, high-impact changes.
  • Automation (robust automation + CI/CD) lets engineers make changes predictably with minimal toil.
  • Key characteristics: loosely coupled services, resilient/self-healing, elastic/scalable on demand, portable across clouds, and declarative (state desired, controllers reconcile).
  • Immutable infrastructure: you replace components rather than patch them in place; new image = new deployment.
  • Speed & efficiency are the business drivers (faster time to market, better resource use).
  • CNCF = Cloud Native Computing Foundation, part of the Linux Foundation, vendor-neutral home for cloud native open source projects.
  • Kubernetes was the first CNCF project to graduate.
  • The CNCF Landscape is a map of projects/products grouped by category (orchestration, observability, networking, storage, security, etc.).

Exam tip: Memorize the five CNCF pillars and the three qualities (resilient, manageable, observable). Cloud native is about how you build, not just running in "the cloud."
Autoscaling (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, Vertical Pod Autoscaler, Cluster Autoscaler)
Autoscaling: HPA, VPA & Cluster Autoscaler

Kubernetes scales workloads automatically at two levels: pods (HPA/VPA) and nodes (Cluster Autoscaler).

  • Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): adds/removes pod replicas based on metrics (CPU, memory, or custom/external metrics). Scales out/in. Implemented as HorizontalPodAutoscaler; targets a Deployment/ReplicaSet/StatefulSet.
  • HPA needs the Metrics Server to read resource usage.
  • Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA): adjusts CPU/memory requests and limits of pods. Scales up/down the size of each pod, not the count.
  • VPA usually recreates pods to apply new resource values (causing restarts). Not a core component; installed separately.
  • Exam tip: Do not use HPA and VPA on the same CPU/memory metric simultaneously — they conflict.
  • Cluster Autoscaler (CA): adds/removes worker nodes from the cluster. Adds nodes when pods are Pending (unschedulable due to insufficient resources); removes underutilized nodes.
  • CA works with the cloud provider (node groups / autoscaling groups) and operates at the infrastructure level.

Exam tip — which does what: HPA = more pods, VPA = bigger pods, CA = more nodes. Karpenter is a newer, flexible node autoscaler alternative to Cluster Autoscaler.
Serverless and Knative / Function-as-a-Service
Serverless, Knative & FaaS

Serverless lets developers run code without managing servers, paying only for actual execution while the platform handles scaling.

  • Serverless abstracts away infrastructure provisioning; the cloud/platform auto-scales, including scale-to-zero when idle.
  • FaaS (Function-as-a-Service): deploy small, event-driven functions that run on demand (e.g., AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions).
  • Serverless is broader than FaaS — it also includes managed backends and event services.
  • Knative is the CNCF project that adds serverless capabilities on top of Kubernetes.
  • Knative Serving: request-driven autoscaling (incl. scale-to-zero), revisions, and traffic splitting for deployments.
  • Knative Eventing: event-driven architecture using CloudEvents, with sources, brokers, and triggers to route events.
  • CloudEvents = a CNCF spec for describing event data in a common, vendor-neutral format.
  • Other CNCF serverless projects: OpenFaaS, KEDA (event-driven autoscaling, can drive HPA + scale-to-zero).

Exam tips: Knative runs on Kubernetes and brings serverless/scale-to-zero. Benefits: cost efficiency and reduced ops; trade-offs: cold starts and potential vendor lock-in. KEDA = Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling.
CNCF community, governance and project maturity levels (Sandbox, Incubating, Graduated)
CNCF Governance & Maturity Levels

The CNCF organizes projects by maturity to signal adoption and stability, and uses open governance bodies to steer them.

  • Sandbox: earliest stage — experimental/early projects with potential. Low barrier to entry; for innovation and early adopters.
  • Incubating: growing adoption and a healthy contributor community; used in production by a few organizations; passed a due-diligence review.
  • Graduated: highest maturity — proven, widely adopted, stable. Requirements include the CII/OpenSSF Best Practices badge, committers from multiple organizations, and adoption by many users. Examples: Kubernetes, Prometheus, Envoy, etcd, Helm.
  • Maturity is assessed via the CNCF TOC (Technical Oversight Committee), which provides technical leadership and votes projects between levels.
  • Governing Board handles budget/marketing/business oversight; the End User Community represents adopting organizations.
  • SIGs (Special Interest Groups) focus on areas (e.g., security, observability) and advise the TOC.
  • CNCF also runs certifications (KCNA, CKA, CKAD, CKS) and the Certified Kubernetes Conformance program for distributions.

Exam tip — order to memorize: Sandbox → Incubating → Graduated (increasing maturity). Know that Kubernetes and Prometheus are Graduated.
Roles and personas in cloud native organizations
Roles & Personas in Cloud Native Orgs

Cloud native shifts responsibilities toward shared ownership, automation, and breaking down silos between dev and ops.

  • Developer / Application Developer: writes and packages app code (often into containers); focuses on features and increasingly owns deployment too.
  • DevOps Engineer: bridges dev and ops, builds CI/CD pipelines, automates delivery. DevOps is a culture/practice, not a single tool.
  • Site Reliability Engineer (SRE): applies software engineering to operations; uses SLIs, SLOs, SLAs and error budgets to balance reliability vs. velocity.
  • Platform Engineer: builds internal developer platforms (IDP) and "golden paths" so developers can self-serve infrastructure.
  • Cloud / Infrastructure Engineer: manages cloud resources and clusters, often via Infrastructure as Code (IaC).
  • Security Engineer / DevSecOps: shifts security "left" into the pipeline; secures supply chain, images, and runtime.
  • Data Engineer / FinOps: data pipelines; FinOps optimizes and attributes cloud cost.
  • GitOps practitioners use Git as the single source of truth for declarative deployments (e.g., Argo CD, Flux).

Exam tips: Know SLO vs SLA vs SLI and error budget. DevOps = culture of collaboration + automation; SRE = a concrete implementation of DevOps principles. Platform engineering reduces developer cognitive load.
Open standards (OCI, CRI, CNI, CSI, SMI, OpenTelemetry)
Open Standards: OCI, CRI, CNI, CSI, SMI, OTel

Open standards keep the cloud native ecosystem interoperable and vendor-neutral by defining common interfaces.

  • OCI (Open Container Initiative): standards for container image format, runtime, and distribution. Ensures images built once run on any compliant runtime (e.g., runc).
  • CRI (Container Runtime Interface): Kubernetes-to-runtime API so the kubelet can use any compliant runtime (e.g., containerd, CRI-O). Dockershim was removed in v1.24.
  • CNI (Container Network Interface): plugin standard for pod networking (IP assignment, connectivity). Examples: Calico, Cilium, Flannel, Weave.
  • CSI (Container Storage Interface): standard for exposing storage systems to Kubernetes; enables third-party drivers for volumes/PersistentVolumes.
  • SMI (Service Mesh Interface): a standard API for service meshes (traffic policy, telemetry, access control) so tooling works across meshes. Note: SMI was archived in 2023; Gateway API is increasingly relevant.
  • OpenTelemetry (OTel): vendor-neutral standard + SDKs for observability — generating and collecting traces, metrics, and logs. CNCF graduated; merged OpenTracing + OpenCensus.

Exam tip — match the C-I to its domain: CRI = runtime, CNI = networking, CSI = storage, OCI = image/runtime format. OTel = telemetry (the three signals).
Microservices, the 12-factor app and cloud native design patterns
Microservices, 12-Factor & Design Patterns

Cloud native apps favor small, independently deployable services built following 12-factor principles and proven distributed-system patterns.

  • Microservices: small, loosely coupled, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and often its own data store.
  • Pros: independent scaling/deployment, tech diversity, fault isolation. Cons: distributed complexity, networking, and observability overhead.
  • Contrast with a monolith (single deployable unit).
  • 12-Factor App — key factors to know: Config in the environment (not code), Backing services as attached resources, Processes are stateless, Port binding, Concurrency via scaling out, Disposability (fast startup/graceful shutdown), Logs as event streams (to stdout), and strict dev/prod parity.
  • Patterns: Sidecar (helper container in same pod, e.g., proxy/log shipper), Ambassador (proxy to external services), Adapter (normalize output), Init container (run before app starts).
  • Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) offloads retries, mTLS, and traffic control from app code.
  • API Gateway, circuit breaker, and service discovery handle resilience and routing.

Exam tips: Stateless + externalized config = easy horizontal scaling. The Sidecar pattern is the most-tested; remember containers in a pod share network and storage.
Observability fundamentals: logs, metrics and traces (the three pillars)
The Three Pillars of Observability

Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal state from its external outputs, enabling you to ask new questions about behavior without shipping new code.

  • Monitoring vs observability: monitoring watches known failure modes (predefined dashboards/alerts); observability helps debug unknown issues by exploring rich telemetry.
  • Logs: timestamped, discrete records of events. Best for detailed, after-the-fact debugging. Can be unstructured (plain text) or structured (JSON, easier to query). High volume, high storage cost.
  • Metrics: numeric measurements sampled over time (aggregatable time series). Cheap to store, ideal for dashboards, trends, and alerting. Examples: CPU usage, request rate, error count.
  • Traces: follow a single request as it flows across multiple services. A trace is made of spans (units of work); answers where latency or failures occur in a distributed call path.

Exam tips

  • Know which pillar fits which job: metrics = alerting/trends, logs = detailed events, traces = cross-service request latency.
  • OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the CNCF standard for generating and collecting all three signal types in a vendor-neutral way.
  • Containers/pods are ephemeral, so telemetry should be shipped out, not stored locally on the node.
Prometheus architecture, metric types, exporters, PromQL and Alertmanager
Prometheus: Metrics, PromQL and Alerting

Prometheus is the CNCF graduated monitoring system and the de facto standard for metrics in Kubernetes.

  • Pull model: the Prometheus server scrapes metrics over HTTP from targets' /metrics endpoints at intervals; it uses service discovery (e.g. Kubernetes API) to find targets dynamically.
  • Storage: a local time-series database (TSDB); data is identified by metric name plus key/value labels.

Metric types

  • Counter: monotonically increasing value (e.g. total requests); only goes up or resets to 0.
  • Gauge: value that goes up and down (e.g. memory in use, temperature).
  • Histogram: samples observations into configurable buckets (e.g. request durations); supports quantiles.
  • Summary: like a histogram but calculates quantiles client-side.

Components

  • Exporters: expose metrics from systems that don't natively speak Prometheus (e.g. node_exporter for host metrics, database exporters).
  • Pushgateway: lets short-lived/batch jobs push metrics that Prometheus then scrapes.
  • PromQL: the query language used for dashboards, ad-hoc queries, and alert rules.
  • Alertmanager: a separate component that handles alerts fired by Prometheus rules; it does deduplication, grouping, silencing, and routing to receivers (email, Slack, PagerDuty).

Exam tips

  • Prometheus evaluates alert rules; Alertmanager sends the notifications.
  • Grafana is commonly used to visualize Prometheus data (Prometheus itself has only a basic UI).
Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry and Jaeger
Distributed Tracing: OpenTelemetry and Jaeger

Distributed tracing tracks a request end-to-end across microservices to pinpoint latency and failures in the call path.

  • Trace: the full journey of one request, composed of spans.
  • Span: a single named, timed operation (e.g. one service call) with attributes; spans nest into a parent/child tree.
  • Context propagation: a trace/span ID is passed between services (via headers like W3C traceparent) so spans link into one trace.

OpenTelemetry (OTel)

  • CNCF project (incubating) and the vendor-neutral standard for instrumenting and exporting telemetry; covers traces, metrics, and logs.
  • Provides SDKs/APIs for instrumentation (manual and auto) plus the OpenTelemetry Collector, which receives, processes, and exports telemetry to many backends.
  • Result of merging the older OpenTracing and OpenCensus projects.

Jaeger

  • CNCF graduated project: a tracing backend for storing, querying, and visualizing traces (Gantt-style waterfall views).
  • Originated at Uber; commonly paired with OTel as the data source.

Exam tips

  • OTel = generate/collect telemetry (instrumentation); Jaeger = store/visualize traces. They are complementary, not competitors.
  • Sampling reduces trace volume/cost by capturing only a subset of requests.
Cost management and FinOps in cloud native environments
Cloud Native Cost Management and FinOps

FinOps is a cultural practice and operating model that brings financial accountability to variable cloud spending, with engineering, finance, and business teams collaborating on cost decisions.

  • Goal: maximize business value per dollar, not just minimize cost; balance cost, speed, and quality.
  • FinOps Foundation is hosted by the Linux Foundation and defines the practice's principles and phases.

Three FinOps phases (lifecycle)

  • Inform: gain visibility and allocation - show who spends what (tagging, showback/chargeback).
  • Optimize: identify savings - rightsizing, autoscaling, removing idle resources, reserved/spot capacity.
  • Operate: continuously govern and improve cost as part of normal operations.

Cloud native cost drivers and levers

  • Autoscaling matches resources to demand: HPA (pod replicas), VPA (pod requests/limits), Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter (node count).
  • Right-sizing requests/limits prevents over-provisioning and waste.
  • Spot/preemptible instances cut cost for fault-tolerant workloads.
  • Bin packing / efficient scheduling increases node utilization.
  • KubeCost / OpenCost (CNCF sandbox) provide Kubernetes cost visibility and allocation by namespace, deployment, or label.

Exam tips

  • Know the three phases: Inform - Optimize - Operate.
  • OpenCost is the CNCF spec/tool for measuring Kubernetes spend.
  • Pay-as-you-go and elasticity make cloud cost variable, which is exactly why FinOps and tagging/allocation matter.
Cloud native fundamentals and the CNCF landscape
How does the CNCF define 'cloud native'?

Cloud native technologies empower organizations to build and run scalable applications in modern, dynamic environments such as public, private, and hybrid clouds. Containers, service meshes, microservices, immutable infrastructure, and declarative APIs exemplify this approach, enabling loosely coupled, resilient, manageable, and observable systems.
Cloud native fundamentals and the CNCF landscape
What are the key characteristics (pillars) of cloud native systems?

Loosely coupled, resilient, manageable, observable, and easily automated. Combined with robust automation, these allow engineers to make high-impact changes frequently and predictably with minimal toil.
Cloud native fundamentals and the CNCF landscape
What is the CNCF and what foundation hosts it?

The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), founded in 2015, is a vendor-neutral home for open source cloud native projects. It is part of the Linux Foundation. Kubernetes was its first hosted (seed) project.
Cloud native fundamentals and the CNCF landscape
What is 'immutable infrastructure' and why is it central to cloud native?

Infrastructure (servers/containers) is never modified after deployment; to make a change you replace the component with a new version rather than patching in place. This yields predictable, repeatable, easily rollback-able deployments and avoids configuration drift.
Autoscaling (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, Vertical Pod Autoscaler, Cluster Autoscaler)
What does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) do?

The HPA automatically scales the number of pod replicas in a workload (Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet) up or down based on observed metrics such as CPU/memory utilization or custom metrics. It does not apply to non-scalable objects like DaemonSets.
Autoscaling (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, Vertical Pod Autoscaler, Cluster Autoscaler)
What does the Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) do?

The VPA automatically adjusts the CPU and memory resource requests/limits of pods to match actual usage. Unlike HPA which changes replica count, VPA changes per-pod resources; applying new values typically requires the pod to be recreated.
Autoscaling (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, Vertical Pod Autoscaler, Cluster Autoscaler)
What does the Cluster Autoscaler do, and how does it differ from HPA/VPA?

The Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the number of nodes in the cluster: it adds nodes when pods are unschedulable (Pending due to insufficient resources) and removes underutilized nodes. HPA/VPA scale pods/resources; Cluster Autoscaler scales the underlying infrastructure.
Autoscaling (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, Vertical Pod Autoscaler, Cluster Autoscaler)
Why should HPA and VPA generally not target the same metric (e.g., CPU) on the same workload?

They can conflict: HPA scales replica count based on CPU while VPA changes the pod's CPU requests, and each reacting to the other's changes causes thrashing. They can be combined only if driven by different metrics (or VPA in recommendation-only mode).
Serverless and Knative / Function-as-a-Service
What is serverless computing?

An execution model where the cloud provider dynamically manages server allocation; developers deploy code without provisioning or managing servers. Resources scale automatically with demand (including scale-to-zero) and billing is typically based on actual usage.
Serverless and Knative / Function-as-a-Service
What is Knative and what are its two main components?

Knative is a CNCF project that adds serverless capabilities on top of Kubernetes. Its two components are Knative Serving (request-driven autoscaling including scale-to-zero, revisions, and routing) and Knative Eventing (event-driven architecture with sources, brokers, and triggers).
Serverless and Knative / Function-as-a-Service
What is Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) and how does it relate to serverless?

FaaS is a serverless model where you deploy individual, event-triggered functions that run on demand and scale automatically. FaaS is a subset of serverless focused on function-level granularity (e.g., AWS Lambda, OpenFaaS, Knative functions).
Serverless and Knative / Function-as-a-Service
What is CloudEvents and why does it matter for serverless?

CloudEvents is a CNCF specification that defines a common, vendor-neutral format for describing event data. It enables interoperability across serverless platforms, event producers, and consumers (and is used by Knative Eventing).

What are the three pillars of observability?

What is the difference between a metric and a log?

A metric is a numeric value sampled over time and is highly aggregatable and cheap to store (e.g. requests_total). A log is a detailed, often textual record of a discrete event, richer in context but more expensive to store and query at scale.

What is a span in distributed tracing, and how does it relate to a trace?

What is cardinality in metrics, and why does it matter?

Cardinality is the number of unique label/value combinations for a metric (each unique combination is a separate time series). High cardinality (e.g. labeling by user ID) can explode memory and storage in systems like Prometheus, so labels should use bounded, low-cardinality values.

Application delivery fundamentals
Application Delivery Fundamentals

Application delivery is the end-to-end practice of getting code from a developer's machine into a running, observable workload in a cluster, repeatedly and safely.

  • Build: source code is compiled and packaged into an immutable container image, then pushed to a registry (e.g. Docker Hub, GHCR, Harbor).
  • Release/Deploy: the image is referenced by a Kubernetes manifest (Deployment, StatefulSet) and applied to the cluster.
  • Declarative model: you declare the desired state in YAML; controllers reconcile actual state toward it. This is the foundation of all cloud native delivery.
  • Immutability: never patch a running container. Build a new image with a new tag and roll it out. Avoid the latest tag in production (non-deterministic).
  • Exam tip — deployment strategies: Rolling update (default for Deployment, gradual replacement, no downtime); Recreate (kill all, then start new, causes downtime); Blue-Green (two full environments, switch traffic); Canary (route a small % of traffic to the new version first).
  • Rollbacks: Deployment keeps revision history; kubectl rollout undo reverts.
  • 12-Factor App principles (config in env, stateless processes, disposability) underpin cloud native delivery.
  • Goal of good delivery: repeatability, reliability, speed, and safe rollback.
CI/CD concepts and pipelines
CI/CD Concepts and Pipelines

CI/CD automates the path from a code commit to a deployed workload, replacing manual, error-prone steps with a repeatable pipeline.

  • CI (Continuous Integration): every commit is automatically built and tested. Catches integration bugs early, keeps main always releasable.
  • CD has two meanings: Continuous Delivery (every change is automatically prepared/staged but a human approves the production release) vs Continuous Deployment (every passing change goes to production with no manual gate).
  • Typical pipeline stages: source/commit → build image → test (unit/integration) → scan (vulnerabilities, lint) → push to registry → deploy.
  • Pipeline as code: the pipeline definition lives in the repo (e.g. .gitlab-ci.yml, GitHub Actions workflow), versioned alongside the app.
  • CNCF tools: Tekton (Kubernetes-native CI/CD using Task and Pipeline CRDs, runs each step as a pod), Argo Workflows, plus ecosystem tools like Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions.
  • Exam tip: CI/CD is push-based — the pipeline has credentials and pushes changes into the cluster (kubectl apply). Contrast with GitOps, which is pull-based.
  • Tekton vs Argo Workflows: both run pipelines as pods in-cluster; Tekton focuses on CI/CD building blocks, Argo Workflows is a general DAG/workflow engine.
  • Benefits: faster feedback, fewer manual errors, consistent and auditable releases.
GitOps with Argo CD and Flux (declarative, pull-based reconciliation)
GitOps: Argo CD & Flux

GitOps uses a Git repository as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and apps; an in-cluster agent continuously reconciles the cluster to match Git.

  • Four GitOps principles: (1) Declarative — desired state expressed as data; (2) Versioned & immutable — stored in Git; (3) Pulled automatically — agents pull approved state; (4) Continuously reconciled — drift is detected and corrected.
  • Pull-based: the agent runs inside the cluster and pulls from Git. The cluster's credentials never leave it — more secure than push-based CI/CD. Exam tip: GitOps = pull; classic CI/CD = push.
  • Reconciliation loop: agent compares Git (desired) vs cluster (actual), reports drift, and applies changes. Reverting a bad change = a Git revert.
  • Argo CD: GitOps controller with a rich UI/CLI. Core CRD is Application (maps a Git path to a cluster/namespace). Shows sync status (Synced/OutOfSync) and health; supports manual or automated sync and self-heal.
  • Flux (CNCF graduated): a set of controllers (GitOps Toolkit) — GitRepository, Kustomization, HelmRelease. CLI-driven, no built-in UI; composable and lightweight.
  • Both are CNCF graduated and natively support Helm and Kustomize sources.
  • Benefits: auditable Git history, easy rollback, drift correction, separation of CI (build/push image) from CD (GitOps deploys).
Packaging and templating with Helm and Kustomize
Helm & Kustomize Packaging

Helm and Kustomize both produce Kubernetes manifests but take opposite approaches: Helm templates and packages, Kustomize overlays plain YAML.

  • Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes (CNCF graduated). A package is a chart.
  • Chart structure: Chart.yaml (metadata), values.yaml (default config), and templates/ (Go-templated manifests using {{ .Values.x }}).
  • Release: an installed instance of a chart; Helm v3 tracks release state as Secrets in-cluster (no Tiller — removed in v3).
  • Key commands: helm install, helm upgrade, helm rollback, helm template (render only). Charts are shared via chart repositories or OCI registries.
  • Kustomize is template-free; built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k).
  • Uses a base + overlays model driven by kustomization.yaml: a shared base is customized per environment (dev/staging/prod) via patches, namePrefix, commonLabels, and image overrides — without copying YAML.
  • Exam tip: Helm = templating + packaging + versioned releases + lifecycle management; Kustomize = patch/overlay plain YAML, no templating language, native to kubectl.
  • They can be combined; both Argo CD and Flux natively support each.

GitOps uses a Git repository of declarative manifests as the single source of truth; an agent (such as Argo CD or Flux) continuously reconciles the live cluster state to match Git. A container registry stores images, not the desired cluster state, and imperative scripts contradict the declarative GitOps model.
A Git repository containing declarative configuration manifests
The kubelet's local cache on each worker node
An imperative shell script run manually by an operator
The container registry storing the application images

GitOps Reconciliation

A team uses a GitOps controller running inside the cluster. An operator manually edits a Deployment with kubectl, changing the replica count, but the value in the Git repository is unchanged. Assuming a typical pull-based GitOps setup with self-healing enabled, what is the expected behavior?

A pull-based GitOps controller with self-healing continuously reconciles live state to the desired state in Git, so out-of-band manual changes are treated as drift and reverted to match the repository. GitOps does not auto-commit live changes back to Git, nor does it abandon Git as the source of truth.
The controller detects the drift and reconciles the live Deployment back to the replica count declared in Git
The manual change becomes the new desired state and is automatically committed back to Git
The controller permanently disables itself because manual changes were detected
The cluster ignores Git from then on and trusts only the manually applied value

GitOps Reconciliation Model
Tools like Argo CD and Flux are described as using a 'pull-based' deployment model. What does this mean?

In the pull-based model, an agent running inside the cluster continuously pulls (fetches) the desired state from Git and reconciles the cluster to match it. This contrasts with push-based CI pipelines that use external credentials to push changes into the cluster.
An in-cluster agent pulls the desired state from Git and applies it to the cluster
A CI pipeline pushes manifests to the cluster using kubectl apply
Developers manually pull images from a registry onto each node
The cluster pulls container logs back to a central Git server

An operator uses kubectl to manually scale a Deployment that is managed by Argo CD. What does Argo CD report about this application?

Argo CD continuously compares live cluster state against the desired state in Git. A manual change creates drift, so the application is reported as OutOfSync. GitOps tools reconcile from Git to cluster; they do not write live changes back to Git.
The application is OutOfSync because live state differs from Git
The application is automatically deleted to protect the cluster
The change is committed back to Git to update the source of truth

GitOps Self-Healing
With automated sync and self-healing enabled, how does a GitOps controller respond when it detects that the live cluster state has drifted from the desired state in Git?

Self-healing means the controller automatically re-applies the Git-declared desired state to correct drift, restoring the cluster to match Git. GitOps treats Git as authoritative, so it never overwrites Git with live cluster state.
It re-applies the manifests from Git to revert the cluster back to the desired state
It updates the Git repository to match the current live cluster state
It pauses all reconciliation until an operator manually approves
It rolls back the Git history to the previous commit

Helm Fundamentals
In the Helm ecosystem, what is the standard term for the packaged unit that bundles all the Kubernetes resource templates and metadata needed to deploy an application?

A Helm chart is the packaging format that contains templated Kubernetes manifests plus metadata (Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/). A 'manifest' is just a rendered YAML resource definition, a 'pod' is a single workload object, and 'kustomization' belongs to the Kustomize tool, not Helm.
A chart
A manifest
A pod
A kustomization
Helm Values
How does Helm allow a user to customize a chart's configuration without editing the chart's templates directly?

Helm separates configuration from templates: defaults live in values.yaml and users override them via a custom values file (-f) or --set on the command line. Charts are not compiled binaries, etcd is not edited directly, and customization happens at render time rather than by manually patching live objects.
By overriding parameters through a values file (values.yaml) or --set flags
By editing the rendered manifests in etcd directly
By patching each resource with a separate kubectl command after install
By recompiling the chart binary with new defaults
Kustomize Approach
Which statement best describes how Kustomize differs from Helm in its core approach to customizing Kubernetes manifests?

Kustomize is template-free: it takes valid base YAML and applies declarative overlays/patches without a templating language. Helm, by contrast, relies on Go-template-based variable substitution driven by values. Both are client-side build/render tools, and neither is limited to only creating or only deleting resources.
Kustomize uses template-free, declarative overlays that patch plain YAML, while Helm uses a templating engine with variables
Kustomize requires a templating language like Go templates, while Helm uses plain YAML patches
Kustomize can only delete resources, while Helm can only create them
Kustomize runs exclusively inside the cluster, while Helm runs only on the client
Kustomize Bases and Overlays
A team keeps one common set of manifests and then creates separate folders that patch them for dev, staging, and production. Which Kustomize concept are the per-environment folders an example of?

Kustomize uses a base (shared manifests) plus overlays (environment-specific kustomizations that reference the base via 'resources' and apply patches). Subcharts are a Helm dependency mechanism, and CRDs extend the Kubernetes API rather than implement this layering pattern.
Overlays that reference and modify a common base
Helm subcharts pulled from a dependency repository

Kubectl and Kustomize Integration
Kustomize functionality is built directly into kubectl. Which command applies a directory containing a kustomization.yaml to a cluster?

Kustomize is integrated into kubectl, and the -k flag tells kubectl to build a kustomization directory and apply the result. ('kubectl kustomize <dir>' only renders to stdout without applying.) There is no 'kubectl helm' or 'kubectl create chart' subcommand.
kubectl apply -k <directory>
kubectl kustomize install <directory>
kubectl helm apply <directory>
kubectl create chart <directory>
Helm Releases and Lifecycle

When Helm installs a chart into a cluster, it creates a named release and stores its state so the deployment can be upgraded or rolled back later. Where does modern Helm (v3) store this release state by default?

Helm v3 persists release information as Secrets (base64-encoded, type helm.sh/release.v1) in the target namespace by default, enabling upgrades and rollbacks. Tiller was removed in Helm v3, so there is no server-side Tiller component, and release state is not kept solely on the workstation or in values.yaml.
In Kubernetes Secrets within the release's namespace
In a dedicated Tiller pod running in kube-system
In a local file on the operator's workstation only
In the chart's values.yaml committed to Git
